howCards.heading: What Is an Online Ruler?
howCards.body: A free online ruler is a calibrated browser instrument that draws true-scale ticks directly on your screen glass in inches, centimeters, millimeters, and CSS pixels. Because web browsers default to 96 CSS pixels per inch regardless of monitor size, uncalibrated tools distort physical dimensions. Local calibration maps real hardware pixel pitch to 1:1 physical length with zero downloads.

howCards.heading: How to Use the Online Ruler
howCards.body: Calibrate once below, pick your preferred unit, and hold any object flat against the workspace canvas. Start from the inset 0 line rather than the monitor bezel so raised frames never clip your edge. Click any ruler strip or stage area to drop draggable blue guide lines that automatically subtract start and end positions into a clear span readout.

howCards.heading: Measuring in Inches
howCards.body: In [[link:/inch-ruler|Inches mode]], every inch (25.4 mm) subdivides into classic 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, and 1/16 graduations for woodworking, shipping boxes, and crafts. Tick heights reflect each reduced denominator automatically. Wide desktop and laptop displays render a continuous 12-inch online ruler span (or expand via fullscreen mode [[kbd:F]]) with decimal and fractional readouts.

howCards.heading: Measuring in Centimeters and Millimeters
howCards.body: Switch to [[link:/cm-ruler|cm]] for stationery, cards, and packaging (1 cm = 10 mm), or select the [[link:/mm-ruler|mm online ruler]] when checking metric screws, watch lug widths, or 3D-printed tolerances. Need both systems together? Enable Dual cm/in mode in the toolbar to inspect opposing metric and inch edges on one calibrated frame.

howCards.heading: How to Calibrate an Online Ruler
howCards.body: Browser privacy limits prevent websites from reading exact monitor panel size automatically. To create an accurate online ruler to scale, hold a standard credit card, debit card, or driver license (ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1: 85.60 × 53.98 mm / 3.370 × 2.125 in) against the calibration box, or enter your screen’s diagonal inches at 100% browser zoom.

howCards.heading: How to Get Actual-Size Measurements
howCards.body: For reliable real online ruler readings, look straight down perpendicular to the tick mark—viewing at an angle through thick monitor glass shifts readings slightly via optical parallax. Verify calibration quickly with everyday US coins: a Quarter measures 0.955 in (24.26 mm) and a Penny is 0.75 in (19.05 mm). Save mechanical calipers for machining tolerances.

howCards.heading: Using an Online Ruler on Mobile and Desktop
howCards.body: Desktop monitors offer wide horizontal strips for 12-inch spans, keyboard shortcuts, and independent profiles saved per monitor. On smartphones and tablets with narrow screens, switch to Portrait Card Calibration (53.98 mm short card edge) and touch-drag guide lines. Active screen size sets the single-pass limit across both form factors.

howCards.heading: Common Measurement Questions

faqs.q: Is there an online ruler you can use to measure real objects online?
faqs.a: Yes. Online Ruler Plus turns any desktop monitor, laptop, tablet, or smartphone screen into a free actual-size online ruler calibrated in inches (with 1/16″ fractions), centimeters, and millimeters. Once you match a standard bank card or enter your display diagonal, tick spacing adjusts to your panel’s physical pixel pitch so you can measure physical objects directly on the glass.

faqs.q: How do you use an online ruler?
faqs.a: First, calibrate your display under Calibrate Your Screen using an ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 payment card (85.60 × 53.98 mm) or your screen diagonal at 100% browser zoom. Second, pick Inches, cm, mm, or px from the workspace toolbar. Third, align the starting edge of your item with the visible 0 mark inside the screen frame (inset from the bezel), then read the opposite edge directly or click the ruler strip to drop draggable measurement guide lines.

faqs.q: How do you read a ruler online in inches, cm, and mm?
faqs.a: Start at the 0 datum line, locate the whole unit number just before your object ends, and count the smaller graduation ticks past that number. On the metric scale, numbered centimeters break into ten 1 mm increments with a taller tick at the 5 mm halfway mark. On the imperial inch scale, tick height decreases by fraction: half-inch (1/2″), quarter-inch (1/4″), eighth-inch (1/8″), and sixteenth-inch (1/16″). Moving your pointer across the stage also prints exact coordinates in the top status bar.

faqs.q: How do you identify 1 inch on an online ruler?
faqs.a: Switch the workspace to Inches (shortcut 2) after calibrating your display, then look at the calibrated distance from 0 to 1—equivalent to exactly 25.4 millimeters (2.54 cm). Do not count 96 CSS pixels on an uncalibrated monitor, because real screen pixel densities vary widely. For a fast sanity check against calibrated screen ticks, a US Quarter measures 0.955 inches (24.26 mm, just under 1 inch) and a US Penny measures exactly 0.75 inches (3/4 inch).

faqs.q: How do you measure cm and mm online?
faqs.a: Click cm (shortcut 1) or mm (shortcut 4) in the workspace toolbar, or launch the dedicated cm Ruler or mm Ruler page. Hold your item flat against the calibrated screen edge starting at the 0 hairline, read whole centimeters along the numbered ticks, and count individual 1 mm divisions to the nearest edge. Turning on Dual cm/in displays both metric and imperial scales simultaneously for side-by-side conversion.

faqs.q: Can I use my phone as a ruler, and can a smartphone measure objects?
faqs.a: Yes, within the physical length of your phone display. Modern smartphones pack high-DPI OLED or LCD panels (usually 2x to 3x device pixel ratio), so an uncalibrated 96 PPI web scale renders too small. Open Portrait Card Calibration (53.98 mm short-edge card outline) on your phone first, then place coins, screws, rings, or cards directly on the glass. Items longer than your phone screen—roughly 13 to 16 cm (5 to 6.5 inches)—cannot fit in a single pass and require stepping along a mark or using a physical tape measure.

faqs.q: Can I use my camera as a ruler?
faqs.a: Online Ruler Plus does not access your camera or process photos; every measurement happens directly against your calibrated screen glass inside the browser. While dedicated mobile apps such as Apple Measure (using LiDAR on supported iPhones/iPads) or Android ARCore rulers estimate room-scale distances through a camera, camera-based measurements are sensitive to lighting, lens perspective, and edge-detection drift. For small parts under a few inches, flat screen-glass contact after calibration avoids depth estimation error.

faqs.q: How do you view or add a ruler in Word Online?
faqs.a: Online Ruler Plus is an independent browser measurement tool, not a Microsoft Office add-in. Inside Microsoft Word for the web (Word Online), switch to Editing mode rather than Reading View, click the View tab on the top ribbon, and check the Ruler option in the Show group to turn document margin and tab-stop rulers on or off. Word for the web shows the horizontal page ruler across the top of the document in Editing view, whereas desktop Word additionally supports a vertical left margin ruler.

faqs.q: How do you show a ruler in PowerPoint Online?
faqs.a: In Microsoft PowerPoint for the web (PowerPoint Online), open your deck in Editing view, select the View tab in the ribbon, and enable the Ruler toggle alongside Gridlines or Guides if available in your current web release. Note that slide rulers inside PowerPoint measure virtual slide coordinates (such as a 13.333 × 7.5-inch widescreen layout) rather than actual physical millimeters on your monitor glass.

faqs.q: Why do online rulers require calibration, and does browser zoom break accuracy?
faqs.a: Web browsers render layout dimensions using a fixed W3C reference ratio of 96 CSS pixels per inch while concealing your monitor’s true physical dimensions for privacy. Because physical desktop panels sit around 82 to 110 CSS PPI and laptops often hit 113 to 142 CSS PPI, uncalibrated web rulers routinely err by 10% to 35%. Online Ruler Plus stores your calibrated physical hardware density (devicePxPerMm) in localStorage and listens for devicePixelRatio changes, automatically rescaling tick spacing if you zoom the page.

faqs.q: Does calibration carry across multiple monitors and stay private?
faqs.a: Each manual calibration saves locally in browser localStorage keyed by your screen resolution, devicePixelRatio, and platform family. Moving the window to a second monitor with a different size prompts or loads that display’s own saved scale profile. No measurement dimensions, camera streams, or calibration values are uploaded to our servers; cookie and advertising disclosures are detailed on our Privacy Policy page.

cards.heading: How is an online centimeter ruler subdivided?
cards.body: An online centimeter ruler is a metric linear measurement scale where every major numbered unit represents 1 centimeter (10 millimeters or 0.3937008 inches). According to SI metric drawing standards, each 1 cm interval is divided into 10 equal millimeter ticks (10% of a centimeter each), with a medium-length tick mark at the 0.5 cm (5 mm or 50%) midpoint for rapid visual scanning. First, open the calibration panel on Online Ruler Plus and match an 8.56 cm bank card to set your pixel density. Second, align your object at the 0 cm datum line. For example, in practice, we found that calibrating your display ensures 10 cm on screen equals 100.0 mm in physical reality rather than defaulting to uncalibrated 96 PPI browser guesses that err by 15% to 35% in 2026.

cards.heading: How do you convert centimeters to inches accurately?
cards.body: Centimeter-to-inch conversion is a fixed mathematical ratio defined by the 1959 international yard and pound agreement (NIST and BIPM), which establishes that 1 inch equals 2.54 centimeters (25.4 millimeters) with 0% rounding error. First, to convert any centimeter measurement into decimal inches, divide the centimeter value by 2.54—or multiply by 0.3937008. Second, to convert inches back to centimeters, multiply by 2.54. For example, our conversion data shows that a 15 cm pocket ruler equals 5.9055 inches (approximately 5 7/8 inches), while a standard 30 cm school ruler equals 11.8110 inches (approximately 11 13/16 inches, or 98.4% of a 12-inch foot). In practice, using Online Ruler Plus in 2026 lets you click the Dual cm/in button to view both scales simultaneously.

cards.heading: Which everyday objects verify a centimeter ruler?
cards.body: Metric scale verification is the practice of holding a standardized physical item against your calibrated screen to confirm 100% 1:1 metric rendering before measuring unknown parts. According to ISO/IEC 7810:2019 specifications, a standard bank or ID card measures 8.56 cm wide by 5.40 cm high (85.60 × 53.98 mm) with less than 0.5% tolerance. First, place a bank card at the 0 cm mark to verify 8.56 cm. Second, cross-check with common household standards: an IEC R6 AA battery measures 5.05 cm long, a 1 Euro coin measures 2.325 cm across, a US Nickel measures 2.121 cm, and an ISO 216 A4 sheet of paper measures 21.0 cm across its short edge. In practice, we found that verifying with Online Ruler Plus takes under 10 seconds in 2026.

On a 15.6-inch laptop (~345 mm width) or 24-inch to 27-inch desktop monitor (531 to 598 mm width), the entire 30 cm scale and beyond renders in a single pass with room to spare.

faqs.q: How do I get an actual-size centimeter ruler on my screen?
faqs.a: An actual-size centimeter ruler is achieved by calibrating the browser’s CSS pixel density against a known physical dimension before measuring. By default, web browsers render 1 CSS inch at 96 CSS pixels (3.78 pixels per millimeter), which causes a 10 cm line to measure anywhere from 6.8 cm on high-density laptops to 11.8 cm on 27-inch monitors. In practice, scroll to the Calibrate Your Screen section on Online Ruler Plus, hold a standard 8.56 cm (85.60 mm) bank card against the screen, and adjust the outline to lock in true 1:1 centimeter graduations for 2026.

faqs.q: How many centimeters are in an inch and in a 12-inch ruler?
faqs.a: One imperial inch is defined internationally as 2.54 centimeters (25.4 millimeters), and conversely 1 centimeter equals 0.3937008 inches (roughly 3/8 of an inch). Multiplying 12 inches by 2.54 cm/in shows that a standard 12-inch foot ruler equals 30.48 centimeters (304.8 millimeters). By comparison, a standard metric 30 cm ruler equals 11.811 inches, making a 30 cm ruler 4.8 millimeters (about 3/16 inch) shorter than a 12-inch imperial ruler. Using Online Ruler Plus, you can toggle Dual cm/in mode in the toolbar to compare both scales directly.

faqs.q: How do I read millimeters (mm) on a centimeter (cm) ruler?
faqs.a: Reading millimeters on a centimeter ruler is straightforward because the metric system is base-10: every 1 centimeter interval is divided into 10 equal subdivisions of 1 millimeter (0.1 cm). Starting from the 0 datum line, each short tick mark adds 0.1 cm (1 mm), the medium-length tick halfway between whole numbers marks 0.5 cm (5 mm), and every tall numbered tick marks a full centimeter (10 mm, 20 mm, 30 mm). For example, an object ending three small ticks past the 4 cm mark measures 4.3 cm, or 43 millimeters.

faqs.q: Can I measure in centimeters on an iPhone, iPad, or Android phone?
faqs.a: Measuring in centimeters on an iPhone, iPad, or Android smartphone works directly in your mobile browser using Online Ruler Plus without downloading an app. Because mobile Retina and AMOLED screens pack 326 to 460 physical pixels per inch with 2x or 3x operating-system scaling, uncalibrated mobile rulers are frequently off by over 25%. First, calibrate your screen and ensure the Left and Right vertical rulers are visible. Second, click the Left vertical ruler strip to drop a horizontal guide line aligned with the bottom base of your object, then click again to drop a second horizontal guide aligned with the top of the object. The workspace readout bar automatically computes the vertical distance (ΔY) between the two guides.

faqs.q: Why does the vertical ruler measure from top (0) to bottom?
faqs.a: In screen metrology and computer graphics (HTML5 Canvas and W3C CSS coordinate systems), the origin (0, 0) is anchored at the top-left corner of the viewport so that scrolling the page or resizing the browser window never shifts the 0 datum position. You can either align the top of your object with the 0 line at the top of the Left or Right vertical ruler, or place two horizontal guide lines anywhere along the vertical axis and let Online Ruler Plus subtract the top and bottom coordinates automatically.

faqs.q: How do I calibrate the vertical ruler on a mobile phone in portrait mode?
faqs.a: Calibrating the vertical ruler on a mobile phone in portrait mode uses the Portrait Credit Card mode built into Online Ruler Plus. Scroll down to the Calibrate Your Screen section, tap the Portrait (53.98 × 85.60 mm) orientation button above the card outline, and hold a physical bank or ID card vertically against your phone screen. Adjust the slider until the vertical box matches your card’s 85.60 mm height and tap Apply Calibration.

faqs.q: Can I display horizontal and vertical rulers at the same time?
faqs.a: Yes. While the Vertical Ruler page starts with the Left and Right vertical edges active for distraction-free height measurement, you can click Top, Bottom, or All Edges in the Edges pod of the workspace toolbar at any time to combine horizontal and vertical scales into a 2D bounding-box measurement stage.

steps.heading: How do you calibrate your screen density first?

Scroll to the Calibrate Your Screen section on any ruler page and choose your preferred reference method: hold a standard ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 payment or ID card (85.60 × 53.98 mm) flat against the screen and adjust the slider or arrow keys until the box matches your card width; enter your display panel’s visible diagonal in inches (such as 14, 15.6, 24, or 27 inches) at 100% browser zoom; or run Auto-Detect Device. steps.body: Zero-datum alignment means placing the starting edge of your physical object directly over the 0 graduation line inside the ruler strip (inset 16 CSS pixels from the bezel corner) rather than pressing against a raised plastic monitor bezel. Align the left or top end of your item with the 0 dashed datum hairline, then click any ruler strip or inside the gridded stage to drop a draggable blue guide line at the opposite end of your object. recipes.heading: Measuring outer diameter with tangent vertical guides
recipes.body: Trying to line a round coin, washer, O-ring, or ring shank up with tick zero often hides the outer curve behind glare. Instead, lay the circular object near the center of the light gridded stage—or over a thin transparent protective sheet if the ring has sharp metal prongs. recipes.heading: Measuring metric thread length and watch strap width
recipes.body: For small hardware fasteners (M2 through M10 machine screws, PCB standoffs, or watch spring-bar lugs between 18 mm and 24 mm), switch to the [[link:/mm-ruler|Millimeter Ruler (mm)]] where every 1 mm division is marked clearly. Rest a piece of sticky note or clear acetate film over the glass so sharp threads never scratch anti-reflective coatings. Align the underside of a flat-head fastener (or overall head-to-tip height for countersunk screws) against Guide 1, then drag Guide 2 to the thread tip. Cross-check pitch count across 10 mm to avoid mistaking an M3-0.5 bolt for a #4-40 imperial fastener.

recipes.heading: Reading reduced 1/16″ imperial fractions reliably
recipes.body: When working with U.S. quilting templates, brass fittings, paper stock, or carpentry sketches, switch to the [[link:/inch-ruler|Inch Ruler (1/16″)]]. Each 25.4 mm inch block is divided into four visual tick tiers: half-inch (1/2″), quarter-inch (1/4″ and 3/4″), odd eighths (1/8″, 3/8″, 5/8″, 7/8″), and shortest sixteenth marks. Moving your cursor or dragging a guide line displays the nearest reduced fraction automatically alongside decimal inches, eliminating mental counting errors such as reading 5/8″ as 10/16″ or confusing 9/16″ with 1/2″.

recipes.heading: Using vertical edges and stepping spans longer than your screen
recipes.body: When checking the standing height of bottles, keycaps, display stand risers, or vertical card proportions, open the [[link:/vertical-ruler|Vertical Ruler]] with Left and Right edge strips active. Press F to enter Fullscreen mode so browser tabs and bookmarks no longer shorten your usable vertical axis. If an object—such as a 35 cm binder or poster margin—is slightly wider than your display, align the start with zero, apply a small piece of low-tack painter’s tape on the object precisely opposite a whole graduation like 25.0 cm, reposition that tape mark back onto 0, and add the second partial span.

calibrationGuide.heroHeadline: Complete Screen Calibration & PPI Measurement Guide
calibrationGuide.heroSummary: Display calibration bridges the gap between abstract W3C 96-PPI CSS reference pixels and the physical millimeter pixel pitch of your hardware panel.

topCards.heading: What is the difference between physical PPI and CSS pixels?
topCards.body: Physical Pixels Per Inch (PPI) is a fixed hardware property determined by a display panel’s native pixel resolution and diagonal size in inches, calculated as [[code:Physical PPI = √(W² + H²) / diagonalInches]]. By contrast, a CSS pixel is an abstract angular unit defined by the W3C CSS Values and Units Module Level 4 specification at exactly 1/96 of a CSS inch (3.7795 CSS pixels per millimeter). When an operating system applies HiDPI scaling—such as [[code:devicePixelRatio = 2]] on Retina Macs or [[code:1.25]] to [[code:1.5]] on Windows laptops—each CSS pixel spans multiple physical subpixels. Online Ruler Plus calibrates in CSS pixels per millimeter ([[code:pxPerMm]]) and stores physical density ([[code:devicePxPerMm = pxPerMm × dpr]]) so your ruler stays consistent across browser zoom changes.

topCards.heading: Why is the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 card standard ideal for calibration?
topCards.body: The ISO/IEC 7810:2019 ID-1 standard is the international dimensional specification governing bank cards, credit cards, driver licenses, and national identity cards worldwide. According to ISO/IEC 7810, every ID-1 card measures exactly 85.60 mm (3.370 in) in width, 53.98 mm (2.125 in) in height, and 0.76 mm in thickness, with a 3.18 mm (0.125 in) corner radius. Because card blanks are die-cut to sub-millimeter tolerances globally, matching an on-screen rectangle to a physical ID-1 card directly measures [[code:pxPerMm = cardWidthPx / 85.60]] on your screen. In practice, this optical alignment bypasses OS scaling distortion, multi-monitor EDID errors, and browser privacy restrictions without requiring hardware lookups.

topCards.heading: How are metric millimeter and 1/16″ fractional graduations calculated?
topCards.body: Ruler graduation rendering is governed by the international yard and pound agreement (NIST / BIPM), which defines 1 imperial inch as exactly 25.4 millimeters and 1 centimeter as 10 millimeters. In Centimeter ([[link:/cm-ruler|cm]]) and Millimeter ([[link:/mm-ruler|mm]]) modes, Online Ruler Plus generates minor ticks every 1.0 mm, medium ticks every 5.0 mm (0.5 cm), and labeled major ticks every 10.0 mm (1 cm). In Inch ([[link:/inch-ruler|in]]) mode, every 25.4 mm inch interval is divided into 16 dyadic fractions of 1/16 inch (1.5875 mm): Level 1 marks 1/2 in (12.70 mm), Level 2 marks 1/4 and 3/4 in, Level 3 marks odd eighths, and Level 4 marks odd sixteenths.

midCards.heading: Which everyday coins, bills, and paper sizes verify screen calibration?
midCards.body: After calibrating via credit card or display diagonal, you can cross-check physical scale accuracy using regulated everyday items. According to United States Mint specifications, a US One-Cent Penny measures 19.05 mm (exactly 0.750 in or 3/4 in) in diameter, a US Nickel measures 21.21 mm (0.835 in), and a US Quarter Dollar measures 24.26 mm (0.955 in). According to European Central Bank specifications, a 1 Euro coin measures 23.25 mm (0.915 in) and a 2 Euro coin measures 25.75 mm (1.014 in). For longer spans on desktop monitors, a US Federal Reserve Note measures 155.96 mm (6.14 in) wide, an IEC R6 AA battery measures 50.50 mm long, and an ISO 216 A4 sheet measures 210.0 mm across its short edge.

midCards.heading: How does Online Ruler Plus handle browser zoom and external monitors?
midCards.body: Browser zoom and multi-monitor window movement alter [[code:window.devicePixelRatio]] and [[code:window.screen]] dimensions in real time. To prevent silent measurement drift, Online Ruler Plus converts your calibrated CSS scale ([[code:pxPerMm]]) into an invariant physical hardware density ([[code:devicePxPerMm = pxPerMm × dpr]]) keyed by display resolution signature in [[code:localStorage]]. When you zoom your browser on the same monitor, the display observer detects that the physical panel signature matches and divides [[code:devicePxPerMm]] by the new zoom ratio. If you drag the window onto a different external monitor, a status banner prompts you to verify calibration for that panel.

calibrationGuide.s6Kicker: Section 06 · Worked Calibration Calculations & HiDPI Matrix
calibrationGuide.s6Heading: How CSS PPI, Physical PPI, and devicePxPerMm Relate Across Displays
calibrationGuide.s6Lead: Web browsers expose viewport CSS pixels rather than raw native LCD/OLED panel subpixels when HiDPI operating-system scaling is enabled. Using the Pythagorean diagonal formula on CSS pixels at 100% browser zoom yields exact [[code:CSS px/mm]] directly, while multiplying by [[code:window.devicePixelRatio]] yields zoom-invariant [[code:devicePxPerMm]].

caveats.kicker: OS Scaling Caveat · Fractional & Custom PPI
caveats.heading: Why card calibration outperforms guessed diagonal entry on scaled desktops
caveats.body: Many users know they bought a "15-inch" or "27-inch" computer, yet real visible active panels often measure 15.6 inches, 16.0 inches, or 26.9 inches—and ultrawide or external monitors sometimes receive non-integer OS fractional scaling (Windows 125% or 150%, Linux Wayland fractional scaling, or macOS "More Space" scaled resolutions that render to a virtual framebuffer before downsampling). Those hidden framebuffers shift effective CSS PPI without changing the physical glass diagonal. Calibrating with a physical 85.60 mm ID-1 bank card measures the true end-to-end rendered pixel ratio on your screen directly, eliminating guesswork in under 15 seconds.

caveats.heading: Why mobile phones switch to Portrait Card Calibration (53.98 mm)
caveats.body: A smartphone in portrait orientation typically measures 360 to 430 CSS pixels across (~58 to 72 mm physically). Because a landscape bank card is 85.60 mm wide, holding it horizontally overflows the phone screen and clips the alignment border. Whenever viewport width drops below landscape card bounds, Online Ruler Plus provides a dedicated [[strong:Portrait Card Mode]] calibrated to the card’s short [[strong:53.98 mm]] height ([[code:pxPerMm = cardShortEdgePx / 53.98]]), letting mobile users achieve crisp 1:1 physical accuracy vertically or rotate to landscape for longer runs.

calibrationGuide.s7Heading: Optical Cover-Glass Parallax & Practical Tolerance Limits
calibrationGuide.s7Body1: Every LCD, OLED, and Mini-LED panel separates its light-emitting subpixels from your physical object by outer cover glass, polarizer layers, or an air gap (roughly 0.5 mm to 1.5 mm thick depending on whether the panel is laminated). Because light refracts through glass (index [[code:n ≈ 1.5]]), viewing an object from an oblique angle [[code:θ]] introduces lateral parallax displacement approximately proportional to [[code:glassThickness × sin(θ) / n]]. At a 30-degree side tilt, even a perfectly calibrated monitor appears shifted by roughly 0.3 mm to 0.5 mm—nearly one-third of a millimeter graduation.
calibrationGuide.s7Body2: To keep readings repeatable within your screen’s sub-pixel resolution: align your line of sight straight perpendicular (90°) above the zero datum tick and again directly above the second guide line, calibrate with a rigid straight-edged ID-1 card rather than rounded paper corners, and switch to physical vernier calipers or micrometers whenever engineering tolerances are tighter than ±0.25 mm.

extendedFaqs.q: How many centimeters are in 1 inch and in a 12-inch ruler?
extendedFaqs.a: Under the 1959 international yard and pound agreement (NIST and BIPM), 1 imperial inch is defined as exactly 2.54 centimeters (25.4 millimeters), and 1 centimeter equals 0.3937008 inches. Multiplying 12 inches by 2.54 cm/in shows that a standard 12-inch (1-foot) ruler equals exactly 30.48 centimeters (304.8 millimeters). Conversely, a standard 30 cm metric ruler equals 11.8110 inches (approximately 11 13/16 inches), which is 4.8 mm shorter than 1 foot. Using Online Ruler Plus, click the Dual cm/in chip in the toolbar to compare both scales simultaneously.

extendedFaqs.q: Why is the 0 mark inset 16 pixels from the edge of the ruler workspace?
extendedFaqs.a: The 0 datum line on Online Ruler Plus is intentionally inset 16 CSS pixels from the top and left borders of the canvas so the zero graduation tick and dashed alignment hairline sit entirely on flat, unobstructed glass. Physical laptop and desktop monitors have a raised plastic or aluminum bezel that shadows the outermost pixel column and prevents rigid objects from lying flat at pixel zero. Aligning your object with the visible 0 datum line inside the workspace eliminates bezel lip interference and corner parallax error.

extendedFaqs.q: How do I measure the diameter of a coin, ring, or circular object on screen?
extendedFaqs.a: Measuring the outer or inner diameter of a circular object such as a coin, ring, washer, or O-ring is most accurate when using two parallel guide lines on Online Ruler Plus. First, place the circular object flat on the gridded measurement stage inside the workspace. Second, click the top horizontal ruler to drop a vertical guide line tangent to the left edge of the circle, then click again to drop a second vertical guide line tangent to the right edge. The bottom readout bar subtracts the two X coordinates (ΔX) and displays the exact diameter in mm, cm, or 1/16″ inches.

extendedFaqs.q: Can I measure objects longer than my laptop or phone screen?
extendedFaqs.a: Maximum single-pass measurement length is bounded by your display panel’s physical width or height—for example, 14.1 cm on a 6.1-inch smartphone, 34.5 cm (13.6 in) on a 15.6-inch laptop, or 59.8 cm (23.5 in) on a 27-inch desktop monitor. First, press F to enter fullscreen mode so the ruler uses 100% of your screen width. Second, if an object exceeds your monitor width, place a small piece of painter’s tape or a pencil mark on the object at a whole graduation (such as 25.0 cm or 10.0 in), shift the mark back to the 0 line, and add the remaining length.

extendedFaqs.q: How do I use the 180-degree protractor and floating ruler overlays?
extendedFaqs.a: Online Ruler Plus includes two interactive stage overlays for non-axial geometry: a draggable Floating Ruler and a 180-degree Angle Protractor. Clicking + Floating Ruler in the workspace toolbar spawns an independent, calibrated ruler bar inside the stage that can be dragged by its body and rotated 360 degrees by its end handle to measure diagonal features. Pressing keyboard shortcut P (or clicking Protractor) opens a semicircular 0° to 180° protractor overlay with a draggable origin vertex and angle ray that reads angles to 0.1° resolution.

extendedFaqs.q: How do I print an actual-size ruler at 100% scale without shrinkage?
extendedFaqs.a: When printing a ruler from your browser (Ctrl+P on Windows/Linux or Cmd+P on macOS) or printing a PDF ruler template, printers default to Fit to Printable Area or Shrink to Fit, which reduces physical scale by 3% to 8%. To guarantee a 1:1 actual-size print in 2026, open More Settings in your print dialog, change Scale from Fit to Page to Actual Size or Custom 100%, and before measuring any part, hold a standard 85.60 mm (3.370 in) ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 credit card against the printed ruler to confirm that 8.56 cm matches the card width.

extendedFaqs.q: What is Optical Parallax Error and how do I avoid it when measuring?
extendedFaqs.a: Optical parallax error is the apparent displacement of a physical object’s edge relative to the underlying LCD or OLED pixel grid when viewed from an oblique angle through the display’s protective cover glass. Because monitor and smartphone glass typically has a thickness of 0.5 mm to 1.5 mm between the surface and the light-emitting subpixels, viewing from a 30-degree side angle can shift your reading by 0.5 mm to 1.0 mm. Always position your eye directly perpendicular (90 degrees) above the graduation tick mark being read.

extendedFaqs.q: How do I use the CSS Pixel (px) ruler mode for web design and QA?
extendedFaqs.a: Pressing keyboard shortcut 3 (or clicking the px option chip in the unit selector pod) switches Online Ruler Plus into W3C CSS Pixel inspection mode. Unlike physical millimeter, centimeter, and inch modes—which scale according to your display’s calibrated pxPerMm density—CSS Pixel mode measures exact 1:1 logical viewport pixels with minor ticks every 10 px, medium ticks every 50 px, and numbered major ticks every 100 px. Designers and developers use px mode alongside vertical and horizontal guide lines to audit responsive breakpoints and component widths.

extendedFaqs.q: How do I reset my saved screen calibration or clear measurement history?
extendedFaqs.a: All calibration profiles, unit preferences, and saved span records live locally in your browser’s localStorage under the keys orp:calibration:v1, orp:preferences:v1, and orp:history:v1. To reset your active display’s calibration back to the automatic hardware estimate, scroll to the Calibrate Your Screen section and click the Reset Calibration button inside the Active Scale status card. To erase saved span entries, click the Clear button in the Measurement History card on the right side of the calibration section.

topCards.heading: What is the 96 CSS PPI fallacy in online rulers?
topCards.body: The 96 CSS PPI fallacy is the widespread engineering mistake of assuming that 96 browser CSS pixels equal 1.00 physical inch on every user’s screen. Under the W3C CSS Values and Units Module Level 4 specification, 1 CSS inch is permanently locked to 96 CSS pixels (3.7795 CSS pixels per millimeter) so typography scales legibly at viewing distance. However, consumer hardware panels range from 81.6 CSS PPI on 27-inch desktop monitors to over 150 CSS PPI on smartphones and Retina laptops, causing uncalibrated web rulers to err by 10% to 35%. Online Ruler Plus was built to solve this flaw by placing ISO/IEC 7810 physical calibration at the core of the rendering engine.

topCards.heading: Which international standards govern our calculations?
topCards.body: Online Ruler Plus derives every tick coordinate and conversion readout from published international standards rather than heuristic approximations. First, metric-to-imperial conversion follows the 1959 international yard and pound agreement maintained by NIST and the BIPM, where 1 inch equals 25.4 millimeters exactly and 1 centimeter equals 10 millimeters. Second, physical card calibration conforms to ISO/IEC 7810:2019 ID-1 (85.60 × 53.98 mm, corner radius 3.18 mm). Third, secondary coin verification benchmarks follow United States Mint (US Quarter: 24.26 mm, US Penny: 19.05 mm) and European Central Bank (1 Euro: 23.25 mm) specifications.

topCards.heading: How does Online Ruler Plus protect accuracy and user focus?
topCards.body: Our architecture enforces three strict engineering invariants across every ruler page. Second, local measurement execution: all calibration profiles ([[code:orp:calibration:v1]]) and measurement history ([[code:orp:history:v1]]) remain inside your browser’s [[code:localStorage]] with zero camera prompts or measurement uploads. topCards.heading: Where can you solve common calibration issues immediately?
topCards.body: Most on-screen measurement discrepancies are caused by non-100% browser zoom during diagonal entry, Windows or macOS HiDPI display scaling overrides, or dragging a browser window from a laptop screen onto an external monitor without switching calibration profiles. Before emailing support, review our [[link:/calibration-guide|Screen Calibration & PPI Guide]], check the 20-question [[link:/faq|Frequently Asked Questions]] knowledge base, or follow the 3-step [[link:/how-to-use|How to Use manual]] to verify your ruler with a US Quarter (24.26 mm) or 1 Euro coin (23.25 mm).

bottomCards.heading: What details help resolve calibration or layout issues fastest?
bottomCards.body: To help our engineering maintainers reproduce rendering, fractional scaling, or protractor interaction behavior reliably, please include five items in your email to [[mailto:support@onlinerulerplus.com|support@onlinerulerplus.com]]: (1) your exact device model and external monitor size if applicable, (2) OS display scaling percentage (such as Windows 125% or macOS Default Retina), (3) browser name and zoom level, (4) the active calibration readout displayed inside the Status Badge, and (5) steps to reproduce the issue on desktop or touch viewports.

bottomCards.heading: How are privacy, legal, and accessibility notices handled?
bottomCards.body: All inquiries concerning privacy rights, cookie consent controls, intellectual property notices, metrology documentation corrections, and keyboard/screen-reader accessibility are reviewed directly through [[mailto:support@onlinerulerplus.com|support@onlinerulerplus.com]]. We review incoming technical and compliance correspondence regularly and only use submitted contact details to respond to your request and maintain accurate documentation across OnlineRulerPlus.com. See our [[link:/privacy|Privacy Policy]] and [[link:/terms|Terms of Use]] for full governance details.

topCards.heading: How are ruler measurements and calibrations processed?
topCards.body: All physical measurement operations on OnlineRulerPlus.com—including ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 credit card alignment, screen diagonal density math, pixel-per-millimeter scaling, guide line span calculation, floating ruler rotation, and 180-degree protractor angle reading—execute strictly inside your local browser via static JavaScript and HTML5 Canvas. Your measured dimensions, screen calibration values, and saved workspace spans are never transmitted to or stored on Online Ruler Plus servers.

topCards.heading: What data is saved in window.localStorage?
topCards.body: To remember your calibrated scale and preferences across visits without creating a user account, Online Ruler Plus stores settings locally under scoped [[code:window.localStorage]] keys: [[code:orp:calibration:v1]] (display density profiles), [[code:orp:preferences:v1]] (selected unit, visible ruler edges, and strip thickness), [[code:orp:history:v1]] (up to 15 user-saved span entries), [[code:orp:theme]] (light or dark theme preference), and [[code:orp:locale:v1]] (language preference). You can clear these entries at any time via Reset Calibration, Clear History, or your browser site-data settings.

topCards.heading: Does Online Ruler Plus access device sensors or collect PII?
topCards.body: Online Ruler Plus never prompts for or accesses your webcam, microphone, GPS location, contacts, or clipboard, and does not collect or pass personally identifiable information (PII) in page URLs, query parameters, or advertising requests. If you voluntarily write to [[mailto:support@onlinerulerplus.com|support@onlinerulerplus.com]] to submit a display density profile or report an issue, your email address and message are used solely to respond to your inquiry and maintain documentation accuracy.

bottomCards.heading: How are third-party advertising cookies and partners used?

bottomCards.heading: How can you opt out of personalized advertising?

To understand how Google processes partner site data, please read Google’s official disclosure: [[ext:https://policies.google.com/technologies/partner-sites|How Google uses information from sites or apps that use our services]].

bottomCards.heading: What regional privacy and consent standards apply?

topCards.heading: What are the accuracy limitations of an online screen ruler?
topCards.body: The physical accuracy of any on-screen ruler depends on user-performed display calibration, operating-system HiDPI scaling, browser page zoom, and viewing angle (cover-glass parallax). While Online Ruler Plus uses exact mathematical constants ([[code:1 in = 25.4 mm]] per NIST/BIPM and [[code:ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 = 85.60 × 53.98 mm]]), web browsers cannot independently read physical monitor dimensions without user verification. Never rely on a browser screen ruler for medical dosing, structural engineering, legal trade metrology, or safety-critical machining where certified calibrated physical calipers are required.

topCards.heading: How should you protect your screen when measuring objects?
topCards.body: LCD, OLED, Mini-LED, and anti-reflective coated glass panels on laptops, desktop monitors, tablets, and smartphones can be scratched or damaged by excessive pressure or sharp metallic burrs. When holding physical objects—such as machine screws, metal hardware, jewelry, coins, or tools—against your display to align with the [[link:/#ruler-tool|online ruler workspace]], hold the item lightly without pressing into the panel, or place a thin sheet of clear protective film between sharp metal edges and the display glass. Online Ruler Plus assumes no liability for hardware damage resulting from object handling.
